steps.title: Ripeness at harvest
steps.body: Germany's top quality level, Prädikatswein, is graded by the sugar in the grapes at harvest, measured in degrees Oechsle. The six levels: Kabinett, Spätlese, late harvest; Auslese, selected bunches; Beerenauslese, selected berries; Eiswein, frozen grapes; and Trockenbeerenauslese, dried, botrytised berries. Minimums vary by region.

steps.title: Ripeness, not sweetness
steps.body: A Prädikat says how ripe the grapes were, not how sweet the wine is. A Spätlese can be fermented dry, labelled trocken, or left off-dry or sweet. Trocken means up to 9 g/l of sugar; halbtrocken up to 18 g/l; feinherb is an unofficial off-dry term. Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese are always sweet.

steps.prompt: Order these Prädikat levels from least to most ripe.
steps.explanation: Each level demands riper grapes; TBA requires shrivelled, botrytised berries.

steps.title: The VDP
steps.body: Germany's VDP, an association of top estates, uses its own vineyard classification: Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage. Its top dry wines are labelled Grosses Gewächs, GG, from Grosse Lage sites. Many VDP members use Prädikat terms only for sweeter wines.

steps.prompt: What does trocken on a German label mean?
options: Dry, up to 9 g/l of sugar

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prädikat levels grade ripeness at harvest, from Kabinett to TBA
They show ripeness, not necessarily sweetness
The VDP's GG means dry wine from a top site
